articles.title: Watch: New York teen reunites with cat missing after building collapse
articles.summary: Rescuers found the pet cat in the ruins of Zariah's apartment four days after she made an emotional plea to the public.
articles.body:
A teenage girl and her cat have been reunited four days after a building in the New York borough of Brooklyn collapsed.

Zariah Coleman, 13, made an emotional plea when her pet went missing after she and her family were forced to relocate when the side of their building was stripped off in the unexpected collapse.

City officials later found her cat, Isaac, in the debris of the their home and shared the reunion on Sunday afternoon.

Eight people died and 18 others were injured when the three-storey building collapsed in the Flatbush neighbourhood last Wednesday.

articles.title: Stephen A Smith debriefs interview with President Trump, warns Democrats face steep challenge
articles.summary: Stephen A. Smith says President Trump was "immovable" in refusing to accept blame for GOP midterm losses during their wide-ranging White House interview.
articles.body:
ESPN commentator Stephen A. Smith debriefed his White House interview with President Donald Trump during an appearance Thursday on " Hannity " and cautioned Democrats over the influence of the party's far-left flank.

Smith said the pair discussed "devastating" GOP midterm losses during a 40-minute, wide-ranging interview and criticized Trump for refusing to take blame, saying he was "immovable" on that point.

"We talked about the devastating losses in the midterms and how the GOP essentially got slaughtered," Smith told Fox News host Sean Hannity.

"I asked him, is he willing to point the finger at himself, and he was dogged … he was immovable in that regard," he added.

Trump repeatedly told Americans during his midterm blitz to vote as if he were on the ballot, but Smith said the commander in chief removed himself from that narrative during their Thursday interview.

"He said, 'I wasn't on the ballot.' I said, 'That makes absolutely no sense, Mr. President. You said, put you on a ballot. That's what you told the American people to do.' He said, 'Well, they didn't do it.' I said, 'Well, what if they did do it and that was the reason you lost,'" Smith explained.

"He refused to accept that," he continued. "His attitude is that the candidates were not that great. If it were him that was running, this would not have happened. That's his mentality."

Smith explained why he doesn't agree with Trump's perception of how the midterms played out and argued that the blue wave stems from Americans being dissatisfied with his presidency.

"I think that he is somebody that is convinced his way is what it is. I just don't agree with him," Smith said.

"I think the American people made a statement against what they were seeing from him in terms of him not having his eye on the ball and coming across as a bit detached in their eyes," he added.

Smith told Fox News that Trump also gave him pushback when discussing the impact of the Iran war and tariffs on voter sentiment and the economy. He also addressed speculation that Trump offered him the role of White House press secretary .

"That was absolutely hilarious," Smith said. "Evidently, they don't know about the life that I live and the kind of affluence that ESPN and Disney have blessed me with."

"I wouldn't take that pay cut for almost anything but the presidency," he continued. "That ain't happening. Press secretary? Please."

Smith, who has lodged criticism at both Democrats and Republicans, warned that the Democratic Party faces a challenge from its far-left side.

"I definitely think that right now, the Democrats have a challenge on their hands because clearly there's a lot of people out there that view the Democratic Party as a divided party," he said. "Now they will tell you they're a very big tent and there's room for everybody, but I think that the progressive left has shown you there isn't room for everybody."

"If you're not willing to capitulate to their desires, their wishes and their ideological beliefs 100%, then they got a problem with you," he added.

Smith called out Democrats who have declined interviews and expressed gratitude that Trump agreed to sit down with him for an interview.

"[Trump] was just very rigid and immovable in his thinking that it was blown by the people who lost and that the candidates on the Republican side simply were not good enough. It was not about him," Smith said.

"I give him credit," he continued. "I asked a question, and he answered, and he didn't run from anything."

articles.title: Will Trump’s lame duck presidency push him further beyond constraints of the law?
articles.summary: Midterm elections have defanged the US president – leaving critics to worry about his next move in his ‘fat Elvis’ stage
articles.body:
It was just before 3am when Donald Trump entered a crowded Manhattan ballroom, greeted by chants of "USA! USA" and theme music from the Hollywood film Air Force One. On stage, two red "Make America great again" (Maga) caps were mounted in glass cases like holy relics.

That was the scene 10 years ago this week when Trump, a businessman and reality TV star, stunned the world by beating Hillary Clinton to the White House. A decade later an unlikely president is serving an unlikely second term. But in the wake of a humiliating vote of no confidence in last week's midterm elections , he now enters an endgame wracked with uncertainty.

"Trump is about to get even weirder and, sadly, more dangerous," tweeted Clinton , who has been a wry commentator on the Trump years, predicting that the president will deflect blame, become more unhinged, demand even greater loyalty from Republicans and potentially launch fresh attacks on Iran.

Political obituary writers have been swift to describe him as a lame duck, defanged lion or cornered animal in the wake of the midterms. The Democrats' 13 percentage point victory was the second biggest of any midterm election since 1942, and the party conquered the Republican bastions of Kansas, Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas.

The causes of the Republican rout were plain: an eight month war in Iran that sent fuel prices soaring, persistent cost of living pressures and a backlash against masked immigration raids that turned deadly in Minneapolis.

The 80-year-old president's response has swung wildly between conciliation, aggression and farce. He told the CBS network's 60 Minutes program that his deportation push was "too tough" while declaring that no amnesty would occur and appointing immigration hardliner Stephen Miller as White House chief of staff.

He publicly invited the job of White House press secretary to "violent fighter and warrior" Dana White of the Ultimate Fighting Championship (UFC), brought him into the briefing room to play out the scenario, then insisted it had all been a joke. He threw his weight behind the defense secretary, Pete Hegseth , who survived an impeachment resolution brought by a maverick Republican in Congress.

All the while he has retreated into architectural vanity projects, including a White House ballroom and triumphal arch in Washington, and increasingly wayward rhetoric that included ruminations about men's posteriors , speeches punctuated by strange guttural sounds and a lengthy social media post about comedian Bill Maher.

Miles Taylor, founder of Defiance.org , a non-profit aimed at countering government corruption and abuses of power, agrees with Clinton's analysis about the finale of the Trump show. He said: "It will certainly be weirder because Donald Trump was always going to end the administration with the bottom of the barrel appointees.

"Like any wannabe autocrat, you end up in the figurative bunker at the end of the regime with the most hardcore loyalists, which tend to be the people who are willing to contort themselves into whatever shape the leader wants. These are the people who have no scruples and are willing to carry out the president's most extreme edicts and, in some cases, are the ones who have been goading him for almost a decade to do the most extreme things."

Miller is the prime example . He has championed expansive presidential power, branded the Democratic party a "domestic extremist organisation", advocated suspending habeas corpus to speed deportations and asserted that the US has a right to Venezuela's oil and Greenland's territory. He supplanted Susie Wiles, whose more measured approach had been seen as a potential restraint on Trump's darkest impulses.

Taylor, a former chief of staff at the Department of Homeland Security during Trump's first term, said: "In my experience with Stephen, he was a guy that was all too willing to walk up to the line of the law and then leap over it and dare the courts to rein us in. That was literally the type of thing he said to me on multiple occasions.

"One of my biggest fears about this next two years is: will Donald Trump cause the ultimate constitutional crisis by defying judicial orders, including from the supreme court, if he doesn't get his way? I see it as very possible because he's got a team around him that might be willing to make the case of why that would be justified."

There is another way for an embattled president to seek a place in history: foreign policy. Presidents approaching the end of their time in office have often turned to diplomacy and international affairs as a means of burnishing their legacy. After Democrats suffered heavy losses in the 2014 midterms, Barack Obama announced the restoration of diplomatic relations with Cuba, secured a nuclear agreement with Iran and helped broker the Paris climate agreement.

Trump has already placed an emphasis on global affairs since returning to the White House last year. Even as Democrats prepare to rein in the president when they take control of Congress in January, Trump will retain considerable latitude to pursue his ambitions on the world stage, from Iran and Israel to Ukraine and China.

Taylor commented: "What he did in the first two years on the foreign policy front could potentially pale in comparison with what he does in the latter two years and that's saying something because he launched this war in Iran.

"But here are things to look for. Does Nato survive this period? Does the United States actually try to go seize more territory? Both of those are things that Donald Trump has talked about doing and been walked back by advisors on over the course of two terms. I'm not sure that's the case anymore.

"But then there's other areas of the world that might be worried about Trump administration inaction being just as bad or worse than Trump administration offensive action, if the Russians try to seize more territory and if the Chinese take Taiwan . On the world stage I would warn our allies, it's about to get very, very bad. And I would say to our adversaries, this is probably the luckiest two years you're ever going to get."

Despite the historic losses, there is little sign of a Republican revolt against Trump. On Capitol Hill this week the party effectively killed the attempt to impeach Hegseth while also electing Jim Jordan , a pugnacious ally of the president, as its minority leader for the next Congress. Most Republicans who survived the midterm bloodbath are from safe red districts and staunchly pro-Trump. The outcome could be more Maga, not less.

Olivia Wales , a spokeswoman for the White House, said via email: "President Trump will continue to enact his commonsense, America First agenda that has delivered the most secure border ever, the largest working-class tax cut in history, the lowest murder rate since 1900, the sharpest drop in prescription drug prices in more than 60 years, and a stock market that has hit record highs.

"As the President said, he is willing to work with anyone who wants to strengthen our economy, lower costs for American families, protect our national security, and improve the lives of hardworking Americans. If Democrats choose to pursue radical-left policies, they are choosing to work against the best interests of the American people."

Some commentators believe that, given Trump's ideological fluidity, a deal with Democrats might be possible.

Bill Whalen , a research fellow at the Hoover Institution thinktank in Stanford, California, said: "If Trump wants to work with Congress, the question is what do they have in common? If I'm running the Democratic caucuses right now, I might think 70-30 or 80-20 is what I want in terms of a compromise, because the president wants to sign something to show he's still relevant."

Whalen suggests an intriguing parallel: "Is Donald Trump at his heart really that conservative, or will he turn out to be a little bit more of a moderate Democrat? Similar to [former Republican governor] Arnold Schwarzenegger here in California, where he gets chastised, and then in his second term, he's governing very much like a moderate Democrat."

Others suspect that Trump, who has placed a red baseball cap saying "veto" on his desk in the Oval Office, indicating his willingness to block Democratic legislation, intends to go out with all guns blazing. Newt Gingrich , a former House of Representatives speaker, predicts an aggressive counter attack rather than a chastened administration winding down.

"I recommend everybody read Trump's book The Art of the Comeback , which explains what he's like when he's right at the edge of being destroyed, pivots and rebuilds overnight," Gingrich said. "You have to assume that he and Stephen Miller are methodically thinking through the comeback. I suspect the State of the Union [address] will be chock-full of things that the American people want that the Democrats will be taunted about passing."

For Democrats, the uncertainty of whether Trump will offer a fight or flight response poses a conundrum. Speaking at the Center for American Progress thinktank in Washington this week, congressman Jim Himes said: "We just don't know which Donald Trump is going to show up. Is it the dealmaker, or is it the Stephen Miller pugilist? On any given day we're not going to know which president is sitting in the Oval Office."

For Rick Wilson , a veteran political strategist and co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, the president has crossed a threshold into volatile decline. "The impulsivity has come not only from his age but from the understanding now that he is an island unto himself," he said.

"He doesn't have that enormous backstop of congressional impunity to work from. That is going to make him do a lot of lashing out and things like we've seen the last few days – going to the podium in the press room and just riffing."

Wilson believes that Trump has reached his "fat Elvis" phase. "He's trying to recapture the old magic. He's trying to get back the old mojo and it just isn't quite there. The crash out of his approval, the loss of his congressional shield wall and the lack of any adult supervision around him now – it's a toxic combination where he's going to feel desperate and angry and crazy."

While Trump grapples with immediate constraints, political gravity is already shifting toward the presidential succession in January 2029. JD Vance , the Florida governor, Ron DeSantis, and Texas senator Ted Cruz were all quick to weigh in with opinions on what went wrong in the midterms. Former state governors Glenn Youngkin and Chris Christie are among other potential contenders.

Can Trump endure sharing the stage in 2028? Wilson foresees a messy spectacle. "He has been the centre of that political gravity for 10 years now. Because he's the devil, he's going to go in and piss on Vance one day and raise him up the next. He'll piss on Marco [Rubio] one day and raise him up the next. He'll try to be the kingmaker."

articles.title: Democrat Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, as vote counting continues
articles.summary: Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska’s Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis, as vote-counting continues in the...
articles.body:
Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is likely to win Alaska's Senate race, according to an NBC News Decision Desk analysis , as vote-counting continues in the state.

Peltola has expanded her narrow lead over Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan with each new batch of votes reported this week. A "likely" characterization indicates that the NBC News Decision Desk has at least 95% confidence that Peltola will win the race.

Alaska's is the only remaining 2026 Senate race in which the NBC News Decision Desk has not yet made a projection.

If Peltola wins, Democrats will have a 56-44 majority in the Senate next year.

The race remains uncalled a week after polls close as votes continue to be counted. Alaskans vote heavily by mail and ballots postmarked by Election Day are counted as long as they arrived by Nov. 13 — and a few days later than that for valid overseas voters.

In a race with such a narrow margin, these final votes are important, especially given Alaska's ranked-choice rules.

If no candidate wins a majority of the vote on the first ballot, the lowest-placed candidate is eliminated and second-choice votes from that candidate's supporters are counted. The process then repeats until someone gets a majority.

articles.title: Offshore oil rigs could be 'toppled' off California under Trump plan
articles.summary: A federal proposal would make toppling decommissioned oil rigs onto the seafloor the default practice. California has 23 rigs in federal waters.
articles.body:
A quiet proposal from the Trump administration could change the way offshore oil platforms are managed when they reach the end of their useful lives, leaving more of them to lie permanently on the seafloor off the coast of California.

Buried within a September executive order about recreational fishing, President Trump directed the Department of the Interior — through its newly formed Marine Minerals Administration — to establish a federal "reef-in-place" program for decommissioned offshore oil and gas platforms. "Reefing" refers to leaving all or part of the metal structures in the ocean, where they can become artificial reefs for marine life.

There are 23 platforms in federal waters off the state's coast currently, eight of which are in various stages of decommissioning. Four others are within state waters.

The Interior Department has signaled that it intends to go one step further. A rulemaking scheduled for 2027 would make "toppling in place" the default decommissioning method if approved. It's largely what it sounds like: knocking all or most of the platform over onto its side to rest on the sea bottom. Though it's been done in the Gulf of Mexico, it has never been tried in the Pacific waters off California, where all previously decommissioned platforms have been removed.

Critics say the action is designed to benefit fossil fuel companies, which have already profited from several sweeping policy changes since the president returned to office last year. Full removal of some of the largest offshore platforms could cost more than $200 million, according to federal estimates.

"Decommissioning via topple in place would be a huge windfall for oil companies in comparison to full removal, allowing them to avoid hundreds of millions of dollars in expenses as well as complex engineering and contracting problems," said Robert Collier, an oil industry consultant who first flagged the plan on his Substack, Offshore California.

It comes as the White House seeks to reopen waters in the Pacific to new oil leasing for the first time in more than 40 years, along with new lease areas in Alaska and the Gulf of Mexico.

Trump's executive order specifies that offshore wind platforms would not benefit from the policy change. The president's opposition to offshore wind is well documented.

Regardless of the motivation, some scientists say the change could be a good thing for marine life. While some habitats can be disrupted when the platforms are installed, many fish and other species have come to thrive in and on the metal structures over time, including different types of rockfish, mussels and anemones, according to Milton Love, a research biologist at UC Santa Barbara.

For this reason, the question of what to do with an oil platform at the end of its life raises interesting scientific and moral questions, Love said. Removing the structure from the water kills the invertebrate life on it, he said, and crews sometimes use underwater explosives in the process, which can kill nearby fish.

"They happen to be living next to a piece of steel, and you're going to kill them for that? I just don't think that's right," he said.

One reefing method is something of a middle ground, and typically involves severing the platform at 85 feet below sea level, where officials say it will no longer pose a threat to ships above. Toppling changes the conditions even more — converting the whole structure to a deep-water habitat.

It's hard to say what that would mean for the platforms off the coast of California, which vary in depth from about 95 to 1,200 feet in federal waters. While hundreds of platforms have been reefed via various methods in the Gulf of Mexico, the scientific findings there aren't really applicable to the Pacific because of differences in species, water conditions, depths and other factors, Love said.

"Putting the platforms in was a great experiment in terms of biology," he said, "and tipping them over would be a great experiment again."

Some environmental and coastal advocacy groups strongly oppose any form of reefing or toppling, which they argue lets fossil fuel companies off the hook for their environmental legacy.

"What they're asking for now isn't even partial decommissioning — it appears to be ocean dumping," said Richard Charter, director of the Local Government Outer Continental Shelf Coordination Program, a coalition of coastal counties opposed to offshore drilling.

Charter said that the plan doesn't only save the oil industry money on existing platforms, but that it also incentivizes new oil leasing. That's because some companies are more willing to invest in remote drilling sites if they know they'll never have to remove their rigs, he said.

The federal government is also approaching the issue another way. A bipartisan bill, HR 5745, would make it easier for eligible oil and gas platforms to be converted into reefs via toppling, severing or abandonment. It provides for transferring liability for rigs to states that accept them into their artificial reef programs in exchange for compensation. Reefed rigs can also provide opportunities for fishing and tourism.

"Offshore energy infrastructure becomes valuable marine habitat, supporting an abundance of fish and other marine life," said Erik Milito, president of the National Ocean Industries Assn., in an official statement about the legislation. "That is especially important in the Gulf of America, where natural reef habitat is limited," he said, referring to the Gulf of Mexico by Trump's preferred name.

"Rigs-to-Reefs provides a proven way to preserve that habitat and extend the benefits of offshore infrastructure long after energy production ends," Milito said.

If the plans advance, they are likely to face legal challenges from coastal groups and counties, and possibly the state as well, Charter said. But any challenges could be slowed by a larger fight playing out over California's coastal authority. The Trump administration is trying to strip the state's power under the Coastal Zone Management Act, a long-standing law that grants California the right to object to projects in federal waters that clash with state policy.

California did establish its own rigs-to-reef program in 2010 under legislation signed by then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger. Platforms may be reefed in place on a case-by-case basis by removing their upper portions, with oil companies sharing some of the cost savings with the state and transferring some of the long-term liability. It does not allow for toppling in place.

Nearly two decades later, no platform has yet been reefed under the program.

Platform Holly, which sits in state waters off the coast of Goleta, is in the decommissioning process and could be a test of California's policy, said Linda Krop, chief counsel with the nonprofit Environmental Defense Center. The State Lands Commission is weighing whether to sever or fully remove the platform and is expected to release a draft environmental impact report early next year.

Krop suspects the state will favor full removal because it won't want to manage the platform and be liable for it into the future. Liability questions aside, she said she is also opposed to reefing and toppling for environmental reasons, including concerns about invasive species and contamination from heavy metals.

"We're very concerned about leaving this legacy pollution" in the ocean, she said. "If it was onshore, you know no one would allow it."

This story originally appeared in Los Angeles Times .

articles.title: Trump's top officials retreat behind military gates as ex-FBI deputy points to what's fueling threats
articles.summary: Scott Bessent joins Todd Blanche, Marco Rubio and Pete Hegseth at Washington D.C. military bases amid Iranian assassination threats.
articles.body:
Military bases around Washington, D.C., have become an increasingly common refuge for some of President Donald Trump's most powerful officials, as threats linked to Iran and a surge in threats against public officials raise security concerns across the administration.

"So you have this combination of a permission structure on the left for violence, combine it with the ability to track it and create a long paper trail, and the numbers explode, and these threat matrices go crazy," former Secret Service agent and former FBI Deputy Director Dan Bongino said.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is the latest senior administration official to relocate to a military installation, joining a growing number of top Trump officials living behind military gates as federal authorities confront security threats that extend well beyond the White House.

"After The Wall Street Journal published an article featuring an online photo that allowed the location of the Secretary's Georgetown home to be geo-located, security concerns began to increase which have now forced the Secretary to relocate to a military base for his safety. The news media has an obligation to act responsibly amid growing threats against public officials," a source familiar with the situation told Fox News Digital.

Threats against Bessent had reached "more than an advanced stage" amid reported Iranian assassination threats , a senior administration official told Fox News Digital on Tuesday, but did not elaborate.

The Iranian threats against Bessent come amid a documented history of alleged Tehran-backed assassination plots targeting senior U.S. officials.

Attorney General Todd Blanche also relocated to a military base from his home around March, a different source familiar with the arrangements told Fox News Digital on Thursday.

The Justice Department charged a member of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in 2022 in an alleged murder-for-hire plot targeting former Trump national security adviser John Bolton, while prosecutors disclosed in 2024 that another Iranian operative had allegedly been tasked with developing a plan to assassinate Trump.

Bongino said federal protection decisions are generally driven by threat assessments that account for threatening communications, social media activity and intelligence gathered by security personnel. Agencies responsible for protecting senior officials use those assessments to determine what level of protection is necessary.

Secret Service Director Sean Curran said last month that threats against the agency's full-time protectees had increased more than 40% from the previous year, with roughly 10,000 threat cases recorded in 2026 at the time.

Fox News Digital reached out to the White House and Secret Service for comment.

"Pretty much, sadly, anyone at the cabinet, or even sub-cabinet level, with any kind of public persona in the Trump administration, needed a detail," Bongino said.

The assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk and multiple attempts on President Donald Trump's life have heightened concerns about political violence, as security officials confront a growing volume of threats against public officials.

Bongino pointed to his own experience as FBI deputy director, saying his security needs were comparable to those of some of the government's highest-ranking law enforcement officials.

"Mine was on par with the attorney general and the FBI director that we had to expand it," Bongino said of his threat assessment and security detail. "It was an independent analysis."

Bongino said social media has made threats against public officials easier to track, but the sheer volume of online activity has also created more work for investigators trying to determine which threats are credible.

Bongino said the disruption to Bessent's personal life underscores the seriousness of the security concerns surrounding his move.

"For him to have to uproot his life. And move on to a military facility where the housing's not terrible in those places, but it's certainly not what he's used to," Bongino said. "This stuff, it's not a convenience issue, I can promise you that. This is definitely serious stuff."

Lawmakers have also raised concerns about security and federal spending. Rep. George Whitesides, D-Calif., secured House Armed Services Committee approval in June for a proposal seeking a Pentagon report on political appointees living in military housing, including the threats justifying their moves, legal authority for the arrangements and rental costs.

Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., also questioned whether the reported transfer of $415 million in Secret Service funding to White House construction projects could affect the agency's protective operations, citing federal watchdog concerns about staffing and resource shortages.

Barry Donadio, a former Secret Service agent who served during the George W. Bush and Barack Obama administrations, similarly told Fox News Digital that the decision to relocate Bessent to a military installation suggests an extraordinary level of concern among those responsible for his protection.

"My first inkling is that the [threat] is so high that they cannot protect him with certainty, unless he is on a military base which speaks volumes for the situation at hand," Donadio said.

Donadio said the move could indicate that officials believe Bessent would be safer on a military base than at a private residence.

"They may have foiled an attack already that is not being publicized, and as an extra measure, have moved him to a military base for protective custody," Donadio said, clarifying that he did not mean Bessent was in custody, but rather under heightened government protection.

Bessent is not the only senior Trump administration official whose security concerns have prompted a move to military housing.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of War Pete Hegseth have reportedly taken up residence at Fort McNair in Washington, D.C., while White House chief of staff Stephen Miller and other administration officials have moved to military installations or protected government housing.

The relocations have not all stemmed from the same threats. Some followed concerns about domestic political violence, while Bessent's move comes amid reported threats linked to Iran.

Bongino said threats against high-profile officials can also extend beyond their time in government, describing an incident in which an individual allegedly appeared at a California television studio with a manifesto threatening him and other officials.

"I mean, this stuff is real, it happens every day," Bongino said. "And when you're living through it and you're not accustomed to it, you know, and it follows you after office too."

He said officials including Bessent, FBI Director Kash Patel, CIA Director John Ratcliffe and Hegseth understood that public service in the administration could make them targets even after leaving office.

Fort McNair, a historic Army installation along the Potomac River in Washington, D.C., has emerged as one of the military properties housing senior Trump administration officials. The installation, which dates to the late 1700s, is home to the National Defense University and traditionally provides residential quarters for senior military leaders.

Fort McNair's residential quarters are divided into two housing groups, according to a 2020 National Capital Planning Commission report, while a 2024 Army filing identifies 27 historic homes built before 1919 at the installation.

The Army's housing website lists 88 historic dwelling units across Fort McNair and nearby Fort Myer combined, without specifying how many are at each base.

The growing use of military housing by senior civilian officials also raises questions about who approves the arrangements, whether officials pay for their accommodations and what impact, if any, the moves have on housing traditionally reserved for military personnel.

articles.title: Transportation secretary says he doesn’t apologize for FAA’s nationwide ground stop
articles.summary: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country
articles.body:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Sunday declined to apologize for the nationwide ground stop on Friday that stranded hundreds of thousands of travelers across the country following a router issue that derailed air traffic control communications.

Instead, the secretary blamed his predecessors and previous presidential administrations that he said did not do enough to modernize the nation's air traffic control system.

"It happened on my watch, but we have to be clear: I am moving at an incredible speed that no one has done at the FAA or in decades, and I'm proud of the work we're doing, the attention we're bringing to this issue," Duffy told NBC News' "Meet the Press." "But I can't apologize for what was passed off to us, and I can't blame Republicans or Democrats because it's all of them."

The secretary also blamed "30 years of a lack of investment," from the country's previous leaders.

"Why they didn't do that I don't know, but they gave me a system that needs to be fixed, and President [Donald] Trump and I are going to fix it," he added.

His remarks come less than two days after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a national ground stop that lasted several hours, leading to thousands of flight cancellations beginning on Friday and continuing through the weekend.

FAA contractor L3Harris was working on replacing a copper line with a fiber line at a remote site when the work led a router to overwhelm the national FAA telecommunications network, Duffy said Saturday.

Duffy also said Sunday on "Meet the Press" that he expects airports and airlines to resume normal operations by the end of the day or early Monday morning.

"By the end of today, into tomorrow, I think we'll be back to normal," he said, adding that Friday's ground stop led airplanes and flight crews to be "out of position."

"It takes some time for the airlines to rechoreograph all of their crews and aircraft. We're going to start seeing things get better today, but I think back to normal tomorrow," Duffy said.

The secretary also demurred when asked whether he could guarantee that a similar travel disruption won't happen in the future.

"First we have to figure out what happened. Was this a faulty installation by L3Harris that was doing their work for us? Was it a fault of the router itself? We have to do that investigation and make sure we take precautions. We don't want to shut down the airspace," Duffy told "Meet the Press" moderator Kristen Welker.

"We're going to figure out what was the root cause and then move forward from there, fixing how we do business at the FAA," he added.

Duffy also reiterated a call he's made all weekend for more funding from Congress to modernize the nationwide air traffic control system, which has long been outdated and faced problems.

"The president, since he came to office, has been pushing for modernization of the airspace. Before I was even sworn in, he brought this up," the secretary said, pointing to $12.5 billion that was allocated for air traffic control improvements in a GOP-backed spending bill last year.

"The Congress was very specific in how I spend that money. I have a certain allotment for radar, a certain allotment for radios, a certain allotment for building new infrastructure for my centers for air traffic controllers. They didn't give me money for telecom. They didn't give me money for new software," Duffy said.

"I'm coming back to Congress and the American people to explain all the great work we're doing right now," he continued. "We're going to spend that $12.5 billion by the end of 2028, but I need the rest of the money for software and a new telecom architecture that will be way more resilient. I need that money so I can start that build."

On Saturday, NBC News reported that on Thursday, just one day before the ground stop, Duffy and Office of Management and Budget Director Russell Vought sent a letter to members of Congress asking lawmakers for $30.1 billion to upgrade the United States' aging airports and air traffic control system.

They wrote: "This investment is critical to complete the modernization of our national airspace — delivering a resilient telecommunications backbone for air traffic controllers, modern hardware and software, state-of-the-art control towers, and world-class airport infrastructure. These investments will address current challenges, including weather-related delays, while preparing the National Airspace System for emerging demands, such as safely integrating air traffic with the growing space industry."

On Sunday, Duffy urged Congress to "just do it."

"I'm doing all I can to keep people safe," he said. "But I'm also telling you, if you don't give us the resources, we can't complete the job. And this is — of all the partisanship — this is the most bipartisan thing in all of Washington. Democrats, Republicans, the president, everyone agrees on this. Let's just do it."

In a statement Sunday in response to questions about how the president plans to urge Congress to appropriate funds for the air traffic control infrastructure, White House spokesperson Allison Schuster said, "The Trump administration immediately stepped into action at the first sign of issue to ensure the safety and security of all Americans. President Trump put the right leadership into place to effectively handle moments like these, and yesterday, all relevant leaders came together to coordinate a plan that put the safety of the American people first."

She added, "This administration will continue to monitor this situation and communicate to the American people through every necessary means."

articles.title: Trump blasts judge’s 2-week halt to his Washington golf project and says administration will appeal
articles.summary: WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a “highly destructive and political decision” from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on...
articles.body:
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump on Sunday decried a "highly destructive and political decision" from a federal judge who ordered a two-week delay on renovations at a historic Washington public golf course that he has been trying to redevelop into a championship-level venue.

In a social media post, Trump said his administration will "immediately appeal, on an expedited basis" the temporary restraining order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes, which she issued just before East Potomac Golf Links was due to close Sunday for 15 months.

"It is in a terrible state of disrepair, as anybody can see by just looking at the pictures that are now circulating all over the Country, and in the Court," said Trump, who spent much of the weekend posting photos on his social media site of the golf course. "They don't call it Trash Island for no reason!"

Trump had announced work on the site along the Potomac River would begin that day despite the legal challenge initiated against the project in February by the DC Preservation League and two local golfers.

The plaintiffs argue that the president's plan would change the character of the accessible golf course and make it unaffordable, something Trump has denied. They had sought the stop-work order, saying that closing the course and launching work on the project would "irreparably injure plaintiffs and the public interest."

The president's public announcements on social media last month outlining the date of the closure of East Potomac Park and linking it to the renovation of the golf course weighed heavily in the judge's decision.

Reyes, in her ruling Saturday, noted that those posts presented a problem for the government, indicating that Trump's redevelopment plan was final and that the National Park Service "will close the Park to implement it."

Both points, she wrote, "favor granting Plaintiffs' motion for another temporary restraining order."

The order is in effect through Nov. 28. The park's redevelopment is one of multiple projects in the nation's capital that Trump has championed to remake the city. They include a large memorial arch, a White House ballroom and the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts, among others.

Reyes' order was the latest in a series of rulings in lawsuits challenging Trump's projects that were issued just hours before construction was expected to begin. A different judge recently ordered a 14-day delay on work for the arch, a decision that came shortly after a key planning commission stacked with Trump appointees approved plans for the project.

articles.title: Behind the scenes of Scott Colom’s viral ‘pick another protein’ ad
articles.summary: Russ Hudson of Columbus, Mississippi, became one of the unexpected stars of the 2026 midterms, with a feature role in an ad that’s since been viewed more tha...
articles.body:
Russ Hudson of Columbus, Mississippi, became one of the unexpected stars of the 2026 midterms, with a feature role in an ad that's since been viewed more than 20 million times on X alone – tipping his head back and exclaiming, "sheeeit."

"It's been crazy. Like, I never expected it to do this," Hudson told CNN in an interview, reflecting on the ad for Democratic Sen.-elect Scott Colom that helped spark one of the biggest political upsets of the election cycle.

Posted to social media on October 13, the ad features Hudson and other Mississippians rebuking incumbent GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for suggesting there are many other proteins to chose from when pressed on high beef prices. "Pick another protein, sheeeit," Hudson says in the spot as he grills burgers. "I'd rather pick another senator instead."

"When I originally told Scott I would do it, I thought maybe like 100, maybe 1,000 views at most," Hudson said. "I never expected it to do what it did. And I didn't have TikTok. I literally had to download TikTok to see what all the hype was about because a bunch of my friends were sending messages like, 'Dude, you're like worldwide.'"

Hudson said that he'd been recognized in public a few times and asked for pictures, "like I'm some superstar or something."

"So it's a little weird. I'm not used to that, obviously," he said.

Hudson, the father of a four-month-old infant and an Army veteran who served in Afghanistan, said that he'd known Colom for a decade, and that his sister had worked with him.

The initial plan called for Hudson's father to appear in the ad, but he was reluctant to curse on camera, so the younger Russ volunteered.

"I just went to his mom's house in the backyard, and we fired up the grill, and they gave me the lines, and we just rolled with it," Hudson said.

For the signature line – the "s-h-e-e-e-i-t," as Hudson spells it – he said they did about ten to fifteen takes, but that Colom said he nailed it on the third.

"That's something we say. And my buddy was talking to me on the phone the other day, and he said something. I was like, 'sheeeit!' He was like, 'There you go.' It's just a thing, man," Hudson laughed.

Underscoring the ad's point, Hudson also recalled saving the burgers he's seen flipping on the grill. "[Colom] told me to save the burgers because beef prices were high. So, I didn't want to waste them," Hudson said.

Asked what he thought of the comment from Hyde-Smith that started it all, telling Mississippians to pick another protein, Hudson said that "it's ridiculous."

"We deserve better than that, and that's why one of the reasons I really wanted to back Scott, you know, because I mean he wants to make things affordable for us here in Mississippi," Hudson said.

He also considered the landmark victory, saying that "it's pretty cool – I know it's gonna go down in history. My mom keeps reminding me of that, and I'm just like, yeah, it's pretty cool to be a part of that."

"But the main thing is, is the goal was to help Scott win this election, and it did that," he said, crediting the advertisement's writers and producers for "all the work."

As for what he'll remember from the experience, Hudson paused for a moment.

"The Mississippi folks will appreciate this," Hudson said, before referencing musician Doughbelly Stray. "[He] did a song one time that says, 'My Mississippi ain't on this map,' and our Mississippi's on this map now. So that's what I remember from it as we put Mississippi on the map," he said.

Ryan Sayles, the creative mind behind the ad, joined CNN's "The Arena with Kasie Hunt" on Thursday and shared more details on the production.

Saying he wanted to bring a "Mississippi feel to it," Sayles instructed the individuals reading the lines to "drag it out so people can really feel how you feel." He also picked the catchy backing track – "Rapper's Delight" by Sugarhill Gang – crediting his dad's influence as a former DJ.

"I was a class clown, you know. I joke a lot, so I definitely think that this helped people look at it and say, "Oh man, this is funny," but that's really how I feel, you know," Sayles said, underlining the importance of humor in political messaging. "Like it was funny, but it wasn't funny, you know what I mean? It was a good way to just get attention and bring national attention to Mississippi."

And Sayles praised Colom for his engagement with the process and willingness to take risks, saying that "he thinks about how he can reach people that normally wouldn't be reached."

Eight days after Election Day, CNN projected that Colom would defeat Hyde-Smith, becoming the first Democrat elected to the US Senate in Mississippi in more than four decades. The outcome ranks as perhaps the most stunning upset in an election cycle full of historic wins as Democrats capitalized on sharp voter backlash to the Trump administration.

In a nod to the viral ad at his victory party last week, Colom stood at a lectern behind a sign that read "picked another senator" as he thanked Mississippians for their support.

articles.title: Russian diesel under Trump deal struggles to reach US market amid legal fears and criticism
articles.summary: More than a month after President Donald Trump announced a surprise deal to import Russian diesel, the oil has struggled to reach the US market amid outrage...
articles.body:
More than a month after President Donald Trump announced a surprise deal to import Russian diesel , the oil has struggled to reach the US market amid outrage and legal concerns.

Several oil tankers that departed from a key Russian oil-loading port — and are believed to be laden with diesel — are no longer bound for the US, according to ship tracking data from MarineTraffic, and US businesses and ports have steered clear of accepting Russian diesel for fear of legal and reputational risks, experts told CNN.

Bipartisan lawmakers and European allies expressed outrage at the agreement that Trump said he reached with Russian President Vladimir Putin to bring tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel into US and global markets. They condemned it as a concession to Russia as it continued its war against Ukraine and warned that those who imported the diesel could run afoul of international sanctions and US law.

One of the tankers, Agioi Fanendes , departed Russia with tens of thousands of barrels of Russian diesel. Its destination was listed as the Port of New York and New Jersey, and it was initially expected to arrive around November 7.

As of Sunday, the vessel was hovering hundreds of miles off the eastern coast of the US. It was officially broadcasting "FOR ORDERS" instead of a destination port. A spokesperson for Eastern Mediterranean Maritime Limited, the company that operates the tanker, told CNN on Thursday that its "discharging port is not confirmed yet."

Several other oil tankers that departed Primorsk — one of Russia's largest oil-loading ports — in mid-October have also shifted away from the US, according to data from MarineTraffic reviewed by CNN. One, the Talisman, docked at the Port of Alexandria in Egypt in recent days. Another, the Leruo, is now heading to Brazil. They had earlier declared their destinations as the US Atlantic coast. Both vessels are under European and British sanctions, and the Talisman is also sanctioned in the US.

A White House official told CNN on Wednesday that "consistent with the deal agreed to between President Trump and President Putin, Russian diesel is on the water and heading to the market, which will ease prices for Americans."

The official did not say the diesel was heading to the US. The person said the deal "was made to add diesel supply to the global market — lowering prices for Americans and the world — which is exactly what will be done."

Trump announced in a social media post on October 9 that he had reached a deal with Putin for Russia to "immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace."

The administration billed the deal, which was announced weeks before the US midterm elections amid steep fuel costs, as a way to lower prices for US consumers. Experts said the diesel would have little to no impact on prices, and amounts to less than a day of US energy consumption.

Questions about legality of importing Russian fuel

Last month, a group of bipartisan lawmakers sent letters to the CEOs of JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Citigroup, Wells Fargo, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, and the heads of Port Authorities of New York/New Jersey and of Houston, Corpus Christi and Beaumont, Texas, warning that they could face legal action if they are involved in importing the Russian diesel into the US.

The Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act of 2022 bans Russian-origin energy products, including diesel fuel, from being imported into the US "unless — following a period for consultation with Congress — the President certifies to Congress that Russia has ceased military hostilities in Ukraine, that Russia poses no immediate military threat to NATO members, and that Russia recognizes the right of Ukrainians to choose their government," the lawmakers warned .

Although the US Treasury Department issued a sanctions waiver to allow the import of the diesel under the deal between the Trump administration and Moscow, the lawmakers consider that sanctions waiver to defy the law.

"Any importation of Russian diesel into the U.S. raises significant legal questions and may be subject to legal action, as well as congressional investigations," wrote Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen, Ron Wyden, Sheldon Whitehouse, Chris Coons, Elizabeth Warren, GOP Sen. Thom Tillis, and Democratic Rep. Gregory Meeks.

"Criminal penalties may apply to any company that knowingly buys Russian diesel or facilitates its importation, and not simply the importer of record," they wrote.

New Jersey Gov. Mikie Sherrill warned her state's port and terminal operators last week that "any effort to profit from the illegal trade in Russian fuel will be met with harsh penalties."

Charles Lichfield, the director of economic foresight and analysis and the C. Boyden Gray senior fellow at the Atlantic Council's GeoEconomics Center, noted that US importers would face "the immediate reputational risk" as well as the legal ramifications.

He noted that a general license from the Treasury Department, which allows businesses to import the diesel without fear of sanctions, would appear to be good protection but the 2022 law is still on the books, which raises questions about legality and the potential for prosecution down the line.

"All of this is very politically charged (and) the volumes are small," he said. "You could make a few million dollars off this shipment, but is it really worth it?"

Julian Hayda, the associate director for advocacy at the organization Razom for Ukraine, noted that "now that Democrats have control of both chambers of Congress, they are most certainly going to launch investigations into these companies, so it's not going to be worth it for many of these companies to buy this vehicle in and when it arrives on American shores."

This story has been updated with additional information.

articles.title: Luis Figo y Gabriel Rufián se enzarzan en X: "¡Lo que se hace por sobrevivir!" y "No todos nos vendemos"
articles.standfirst: El exfutbolista ha respondido con dureza al portavoz de ERC después de que ironizara sobre su posible nombramiento como ministro de Deportes en un Gobierno de PP y Vox
articles.summary: El exfutbolista ha respondido con dureza al portavoz de ERC después de que ironizara sobre su posible nombramiento como ministro de Deportes en un Gobierno de PP y Vox
articles.body: El político catalán Gabriel Rufián y el exfutbolista portugués Luis Figo han protagonizado un enfrentamiento en redes sociales después de que el portavoz de ERC en el Congreso de los Diputados bromeara sobre el posible futuro del exfutbolista en un hipotético Gobierno de coalición entre el Partido Popular y Vox. El intercambio de mensajes, que ha tenido lugar este domingo en X, antes Twitter, ha dejado varios reproches personales entre ambos. El origen de la polémica está en un mitin de Esquerra Republicana de Catalunya celebrado este viernes, en el que Gabriel Rufián, cabeza de lista de ERC a las elecciones generales del próximo 29 de noviembre, ironizó sobre los posibles nombramientos de un Ejecutivo formado por PP y Vox. Entre ellos, mencionó a Luis Figo como futuro ministro de Deportes. El comentario no ha pasado inadvertido para el exjugador del Real Madrid y del Barcelona, que este domingo ha decidido contestar directamente al político a través de su cuenta de X. Luis Figo le recuerda a Gabriel Rufián su pasado político En su publicación, Luis Figo ha respondido con un mensaje en el que cuestiona la trayectoria política del diputado y sus recientes movimientos para aglutinar a distintas formaciones de izquierdas. "¿Ya me echabas de menos? Bueno, cómo has acabado, chaval, de querer juntar a toda la izquierda a juntarte con Podemos. ¡Lo que se hace por sobrevivir!", ha escrito el exjugador. Luis Figo también ha aprovechado para recordar a Gabriel Rufián su candidatura a la alcaldía de Santa Coloma de Gramenet, en un mensaje en el que le acusa de vivir de la política: "Ya tienes una mala experiencia cuando fuiste candidato a la Alcaldía de Santa Coloma de Gramenet, ¿te acuerdas? Lo que se hace para vivir del cuento, pero ya no engañas a nadie. Suerte para el 29". La respuesta de Gabriel Rufián La contestación de Luis Figo ha tenido una rápida réplica por parte de Gabriel Rufián, que pocos minutos después ha publicado un mensaje en su perfil de X dirigido al exfutbolista. "No todos nos vendemos, as", ha escrito el político catalán, en una respuesta breve y contundente que parece aludir a la polémica que rodeó el fichaje del portugués por el Real Madrid en el año 2000, cuando abandonó el Barcelona para incorporarse al club blanco. De esta manera, el intercambio ha terminado, por el momento, con un nuevo reproche de Gabriel Rufián a Luis Figo, después de que la broma sobre su hipotético nombramiento como ministro de Deportes acabara convirtiéndose en un cruce de acusaciones personales en las redes sociales.

articles.title: As Trump administration implores Congress for additional FAA funding, Democrats say the agency already has it
articles.summary: Following a historic airspace meltdown on Friday that grounded all flights nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has implored Congress to authorize...
articles.body:
Following a historic airspace meltdown on Friday that grounded all flights nationwide, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy has implored Congress to authorize tens of billions of dollars in additional funding for the Federal Aviation Administration.

But Democrats, who are set to take the majority in January, are pointing to legislation passed by Republicans last year that already gave the agency $12.5 billion, arguing that it already has the funds it needs.

"I have no money in that $12.5 billion that I can use for a new architecture for telecom. I can't build new software to manage our airplanes in the airspace because it dates back to the 1990s, but there's no money for that. There's no money for towers. Our towers are old," Duffy said on CNN's "State of the Union" with Dana Bash on Sunday.

Duffy had asked Congress for around $30 billion but after Friday's incident, he upped the request to $50 billion. President Donald Trump, in a social media post on Sunday, also urged Congress to "give the money, FAST!"

The transportation secretary said the ground stop was likely due to an issue that occurred while contractor L3Harris was switching an old copper wire at an air traffic location in El Dorado, Arkansas, to a more modern fiber optic system. It is unclear whether the outage was due to faulty equipment or contractor error.

Of the $12.5 billion given to the agency for three years under Trump's massive spending and policy bill — which no Democrats supported — $4.75 billion was allocated for "telecommunications infrastructure modernization and systems upgrades." Duffy said at a news conference Saturday that the agency has spent about one-third of the modernization budget so far.

On Sunday, Duffy said all the telecom work can be done by "the first part of 2029."

"All I need is the money to finish it. And my, my hope is that if they give me money today, I'll be going tomorrow to build it," Duffy said.

Later Saturday, Reps. Rick Larsen and André Carson — the top Democrats on two House panels overseeing the aviation industry — asked the administration to explain to Congress why the agency needs more money if there are still unspent funds. The two added in a joint statement that FAA and DOT employees will brief their staff on Monday.

Meanwhile, some Democrats slammed the administration's priorities and how it has spent money in immigration enforcement and construction projects in Washington, DC, over aviation modernization and safety.

"There is a pot of 60 billion extra dollars on top of the regularly appropriated amount for ICE and we should use at least a portion of that money for the FAA," Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz said in a post on X . "We can solve this problem and not spend any additional taxpayer dollars."

Illinois Sen. Tammy Duckworth said in a post on X , "You've literally controlled Congress for the past two years. And apparently, there's always been money for vanity projects. But none to fix our air traffic control system? Perhaps Trump should prioritize aviation safety over his pathetic Arch."

Rep. Rosa DeLauro, the House Appropriations Committee's top Democrat, called Duffy's $50 billion request a "ransom."

"Our air traffic controllers have been failed by Secretary Duffy," DeLauro said in a post on X, adding, "We need a competent partner at DOT."

However, Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen, a Democrat who launched a bid for Senate majority leader last week, signaled openness to supporting additional funds for the agency on Sunday while calling on administration officials to come to Congress and "justify" the ask.

"I will support whatever level of money is necessary to fix this problem. We should fix this problem on a bipartisan basis," Hollen told CNN on Sunday, but added, "It's really rich to hear the secretary pointing the fingers at Congress when Congress has given the administration what they asked for. If they need more, they should come up and justify it."

Republicans could use the remaining weeks of their majority to approve additional funding for the agency, and outgoing House Speaker Mike Johnson said Saturday that he would add FAA funding to an upcoming "legislative package."

"We don't really need any investigation to understand we need further investment," Johnson told Fox News. "We're going to work to get it done."

It was not immediately clear to congressional aides how leaders will pass new funding. Currently, appropriators are negotiating a government funding deal ahead of a December 11 deadline. Senate leadership aides in each party did not immediately respond to questions about the path forward in that chamber.

GOP Sen. Eric Schmitt is also pushing for passage of his bill, the Modern Skies Act , which would invest $30 billion in modernizing the nation's aviation system. The Missouri senator spoke with Trump on Friday, and has also spoken with Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on the topic.

CNN's Ellis Kim, Ted Barrett, Logan Schiciano, Isa Mudannayake and Aleena Fayaz contributed to this report.

articles.title: White House calls DC policies 'insanity' after 19-year-old gunman gets probation in shooting
articles.summary: A 19-year-old who prosecutors said fired more than 20 rounds into a D.C. neighborhood got probation, prompting the White House to slam the city's crime policies.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE – A 19-year-old who authorities say fired more than 20 rounds into a Washington, D.C., neighborhood and wounded a boy playing basketball has been released on probation, prompting the White House to denounce the city’s sentencing policies as "insanity." Prosecutors wanted Darius Drew behind bars for five years. Instead, a judge suspended a two-year prison sentence and ordered 18 months of supervised probation under the Youth Rehabilitation Act, a D.C. law U.S. Attorney Jeanine Pirro had previously urged lawmakers to overhaul. "The case illustrates the insanity of Washington, D.C.’s soft-on-crime policies that allow adults to receive just a slap on the wrist for dangerous crimes like firing twenty rounds of ammunition into the community," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital. TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS "It is remarkable that even with these types of radical policies in place, President Trump’s Safe and Beautiful Task Force has been able to drive down violent crime in our nation’s capital," Bis added. Superior Court Judge Jennifer Di Toro granted Drew sentencing treatment under the Youth Rehabilitation Act over the government’s objection, according to federal prosecutors. Drew pleaded guilty Aug. 10 to aggravated assault and carrying a pistol without a license. CHAOTIC TEEN BRAWL GOES VIRAL AFTER TEEN TERROR PROMPTS US ATTORNEY PIRRO'S PLAN TO PROSECUTE PARENTS He was released Friday after spending nearly six months in custody following his May 22 arrest. Prosecutors opposed his release as well as the use of the youth sentencing law. The gunfire that put him there came from two locations in a Northwest Washington neighborhood, according to the government’s evidence. MARYLAND MAN ACCUSED OF GIRL'S FATAL SHOOTING RELEASED FROM PRISON DAYS BEFORE On May 11, Drew rode a Lime bike into an alley before surveillance video captured him firing at a parked car, prosecutors said. The ShotSpotter gunfire detection system registered 10 shots. Seconds later, Drew fired toward a nearby house. A boy playing basketball at a recreation center was struck in the leg. By the time the shooting stopped, Drew had fired more than 20 rounds into the community, prosecutors said. Investigators later found two firearms, ammunition and large amounts of suspected narcotics and marijuana at his home. REPEAT OFFENDER ACCUSED OF SHOOTING NATIONAL GUARD MEMBER HAS LENGTHY HISTORY WITH THE LAW, RECORDS SHOW The probation ruling echoes a warning Pirro delivered to the D.C. Council more than a year earlier. In an Aug. 6, 2025, letter, she urged lawmakers to overhaul the Youth Rehabilitation Act, citing a separate case in which another 19-year-old received probation after shooting someone in the chest aboard a Metrobus. SENATOR TIM SHEEHY: SOFT-ON-CRIME JUDGES NEED CONSEQUENCES. THE JAIL ACT DELIVERS The law, which the D.C. articles.title: Cassidy says questions remain about Trump’s FDA pick ahead of committee vote
articles.summary: Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) on Sunday said there are still questions left unanswered about Heidi Overton, President Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), ahead of the Senate Health Committee’s vote on her nomination this week. CBS News’s Margaret Brennan asked Cassidy during his appearance on “Face the Nation” if Overton will…
articles.body:
Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.) on Sunday said there are still questions left unanswered about Heidi Overton, President Trump’s pick to lead the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), ahead of the Senate Health Committee’s vote on her nomination this week.

CBS News’s Margaret Brennan asked Cassidy during his appearance on “Face the Nation” if Overton will be approved with Wednesday’s vote, noting how the senator said her role in reshaping the Trump administration’s vaccine policies were “almost disqualifying.”

“I don’t know that,” Cassidy, who chairs the health committee, said Sunday. “I’ve been working the phones all week. Both speaking with Dr. Overton, speaking with others. I still have questions. And so, I cannot tell you the outcome of that vote right now. But I spoke to four or five of my down-dais Republican members, as well as continuing to discuss things with my advisers. So, I can’t tell you that answer yet.”

Brennan asked if he might leave the Senate in January without an FDA commissioner in place and if that worried him. Cassidy said yes, “but we’re not going to have perfection.”

“So, then the question is, do we want a series of short-term administrators who probably will have more influence from the secretary, as opposed to someone who may be not, you know, the perfect candidate in somebody’s mind but at least would be a permanent one and have the ability to establish some independence,” the Louisiana Republican continued.

Cassidy added that he “heard from a lot of people who are significant –– who think deeply about the FDA, who have said it’s better to have a steady hand,” though others have offered a “different opinion.”

Overton pushed back on Trump’s false claims that the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine could be dangerous and said at her September confirmation hearing that the vaccine was “safe and effective.”

Republicans are racing to confirm as many of Trump’s nominees before Democrats take power next year. But the GOP has just a single vote majority on the panel, so losing one member would be enough to sink the nomination if all Democrats oppose it.

Cassidy previously said he met with Overton last Tuesday but remained undecided. He seemingly tied her and National Science Foundation nominee Jim O’Neill to promises Health and Human Services (HHS) Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. made in locking the deciding vote from Cassidy before his own confirmation, which have since been broken.

Overton is a top domestic policy adviser at the White House and a former chief policy adviser at a conservative think tank. If confirmed, the openly anti-abortion Overton would inherit the FDA’s safety review of the abortion pill mifepristone.

Trump nominated Overton about three months after the resignation of former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary, Trump’s first confirmed pick to lead the agency.

articles.title: Trump plans to take Qatari jet to Asia, but it’s unclear whether it’s been ‘maxed out’
articles.summary: President Donald Trump is expected to take the Qatari-gifted Air Force One to Asia on Monday as questions linger about upgrades the White House said were needed after a security threat from Iran forced the president to fly home from Turkey on a secret military plane in July, according to two U.S. officials.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is expected to take the Qatari-gifted Air Force One to Asia on Monday as questions linger about upgrades the White House said were needed after a security threat from Iran forced the president to fly home from Turkey on a secret military plane in July, according to two U.S. officials. For months, Trump has said the jet from the Qataris would be “going away” to get “maxed out” so it could “go into any territory.” In September, he said those changes to the plane would “take about 60 days.” The president flew on the new Air Force One to Ireland that month without any issues. He then used the plane regularly during a midterm travel blitz in October, which meant it was not out of commission for an extended period. Instead, the plane has received some improvements and periodic maintenance, but it is unclear whether it has been fully “maxed out,” per the officials. A longer upgrade period is expected in the future, according to one of the officials, but those upgrades will not take a full 60 days. In recent months, the plane has received some “cosmetic” enhancements to the interior, the other U.S. official said, but that did not cover the larger work that the White House said would take place eventually. “We don’t comment on specific upgrades or modifications to Air Force Once,” a senior administration official told NBC News in a statement. “We maintain a consistent posture that ensures a safe, secure, and reliable capability for the President of the United States and routinely evolve the capability as required to maintain that posture. It is the greatest Presidential plane ever built.” In July, Trump said the plane “has a lot of capability.” “But as I understand it, in about a month ​or so, they’re gonna send it to have it be maxed out,” he said. “It’ll take about a month.” Trump did not detail the nature of the work, and the White House has not explained why the original assessment of 30 days later doubled to 60 days. At the time, then-White House press secretary Karoline Leavitt said in a statement that the new Air Force One was “perfectly safe” for domestic and overseas travel but noted in July that the plane would “receive additional upgrades and enhancements in the fall which will take approximately one month to complete.”

articles.title: US airports expected to return to normal after three days of disruption
articles.summary: US air travel was expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US a...
articles.body:
US air travel was expected to return to normal on Monday after three days of widespread disruption following an extraordinary no-takeoff order issued by US aviation authorities.

The ground stop issued Friday afternoon was only the second time such a directive had been issued nationwide in the busy US airspace since planes were grounded following the 9/11 attacks, and was blamed by the Trump administration on a faulty upgrade to communications equipment.

As of Sunday evening more than 55 US-related flights -- those traveling within, into or out of the United States -- scheduled for Monday were cancelled, according to industry tracker FlightAware.

That marked a dramatic shift from the more than 1,960 flights cancelled on Sunday.

The Trump administration sought to reassure weary flyers as questions remained over how such chaos could unfold in the world's largest economy, a country that prides itself on its technological prowess.

Throughout the weekend, stranded passengers wandered through chaotic airports and sat on floors, waiting for updates or to be rebooked.

Officials blamed Friday's colossal snafu on faulty work to upgrade air traffic control communication cables.

President Donald Trump on Sunday ended uncharacteristic days of silence on the ground stop, but only to blame his predecessor Joe Biden for the debacle.

Trump insisted he inherited a mess from the Biden administration and said Congress, which his party has controlled for two years, must approve funds to upgrade America's outdated air traffic control system.

"The Biden Administration was an FAA disaster," Trump said, referring to the Federal Aviation Administration.

"Everything they touched turned bad. Big money spent unwisely, making an old and broken system worse than when they began," Trump asserted.

FAA chief Bryan Bedford had said Saturday that air travel for millions of Americans stranded at airports would return to normal by the close of business on Sunday.

But Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Sunday morning it will actually take longer to get planes, crews and travelers to where they need to be.

"So, in the airspace, we're going to see things come back to normal today, but probably fully normal tomorrow," Duffy said on ABC News.

"We had airplanes and crews out of position because of Friday, so it takes a little bit of time to do that."

Duffy also flatly rejected calls for his resignation over the travel chaos, insisting he inherited woefully outdated air traffic control infrastructure, such as, he said, radar equipment that dates back to the 1960s.

"So when we do work and things go wrong, of course I'm the secretary. But I also have to acknowledge what was delivered to me," Duffy said in an interview on CNN.

The ground stop not only plunged US air travel into chaos, it also raised serious concerns about the country's aging infrastructure.

Duffy has appealed for $50 billion in funds to upgrade and modernize the air traffic control system, and called for Congress, which controls the purse strings of the US government, to "meet this moment."

But Democrats quickly pounced to say Congress under Trump's Republicans could already have done this.

articles.standfirst: Para o desembarque, navio que trouxe a estrutura até Santa Catarina será submerso.
articles.summary: Para o desembarque, navio que trouxe a estrutura até Santa Catarina será submerso.
articles.body:
O Porto de Navegantes , no Litoral Norte, recebeu no sábado (14) dois novos guindastes elétricos de cais. As estruturas, que têm 55 metros de altura, capacidade para erguer até 100 toneladas e podem atender navios de até 400 metros, vieram de Xangai , na China, em uma viagem que durou 55 dias .

🚢 🏗️ 🌊O desembarque está previsto para começar nesta segunda-feira (16). De acordo com a Portonave, nome da estrutura particular na cidade, para a ação, o navio que trouxe a estrutura até Santa Catarina será submerso ( leia mais detalhes abaixo ).

Os guindastes do tipo STS (Ship-to-Shore) farão a movimentação de contêineres entre as embarcações e o cais. Eles foram soldados no navio Zhen Hua 15, que partiu da China em 21 de setembro. Segundo o porto, o investimento total nos equipamentos foi de R$ 229 milhões.

Fabricados pela chinesa ZPMC, os aparelhos têm cores diferentes das estruturas já existentes no local. As lanças são brancas e vermelhas para garantir a segurança aérea , devido à proximidade do terminal com o Aeroporto Internacional Ministro Victor Konder.

Porto de SC recebe guindastes de R$ 229 milhões vindos da China após viagem de 55 dias — Foto: Portonave/Divulgação

Desembarque vai durar 5 dias e terá navio parcialmente submerso

De acordo com a administração do porto, o desembarque deve durar cinco dias. Durante a operação, o navio que transportou os guindastes será parcialmente submerso em uma operação complexa. A expectativa é que as novas estruturas comecem a operar até 31 de dezembro.

🌊 Submersão parcial: o navio absorve água do rio para baixar de nível e viabilizar a retirada das estruturas;

🛠️ Montagem de vigas: estruturas metálicas e sistemas de ancoragem temporária serão montados sobre os trilhos do cais para a remoção dos aparelhos;

⛓️‍💥 Soltura: cada guindaste será solto e, depois, levado ao pátio de cargas.

Segundo a Portonave, a chegada dos novos guindastes é um dos momentos mais aguardados do terminal, que atualmente passa por investimentos em infraestrutura e tecnologia superiores a R$ 2 bilhões.
